subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: If y₁, y₂, y₃ are the y-coordinates of the vertices of the triangle inscribed in the parabola y² = 4ax then show that the area of the triangle is (1/8a)|(y₁−y₂)(y₂−y₃)(y₃−y₁)| square units.

mark_split.label: Take the vertices in parametric form
Set up the area determinant and factor it

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Maths-2B, book p.25 — LAQ chapter 2 Parabola, answer 14, on a printed Super Scoring Page (SSP 25) with the printed aside 'WHAT AN EASY SOLUTION!'. Printed appearance: TS 2015. This is one of the chapter's Five STAR Q's (see the standard-form-derivation card's note). THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS — no margin mark tags are printed for this answer; the split below follows the proof's natural stages. NOTATION: the book's own working uses a 2×2 determinant of coordinate differences (not a 3×3 one) to reach the area — one line of that determinant is typeset here with render:katex, since a determinant's row/column layout has no honest single-line Unicode form; every other line stays plain Unicode. No two-book union check was possible for Maths-2B (no second-year TSBIE Basic Learning Material is on hand), and no board back-test beyond diffing against this book's own five Guess Papers.

steps.label: Take the vertices in parametric form
steps.margin_note: One mark, for stating the parametric form correctly.
steps.why: Every point on y² = 4ax can be written as (at², 2at) for some parameter t, so writing all three vertices this way turns the geometry into pure algebra in t₁, t₂, t₃.
common_mistakes: Writing the parametric point as (2at, at²) with the two coordinates swapped.
Using a different letter a for each vertex instead of one shared a with three different parameters t.
steps.memory_tip: One shared a, three different t's — (at², 2at) is the address of any point on y² = 4ax.

steps.label: Set up and factor the area determinant
steps.margin_note: Three marks. This is the heart of the proof — the determinant, then the two factorings.

lines.text: \text{Area of }\triangle PQR = \frac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix} x_1-x_2 & x_1-x_3 \\ y_1-y_2 & y_1-y_3 \end{vmatrix}

steps.why: Each column of the determinant shares a factor — the first column shares (t₁−t₂), the second shares (t₁−t₃) — and pulling those factors out front leaves a much smaller expression, (t₁+t₂) − (t₁+t₃), which simplifies to t₂−t₃.
common_mistakes: Not spotting the common factor in each column and trying to expand the determinant by brute force instead.
Losing a sign when pulling (t₁−t₂) or (t₁−t₃) out of its column.
steps.memory_tip: Each column of this determinant is a difference of squares in disguise — pulling out the common factor from each column is what shrinks it.

steps.label: Convert t-differences to y-differences
steps.margin_note: Two marks for the substitution that brings y₁, y₂, y₃ back into the answer.
steps.why: The parameter t was only ever a convenient stand-in for y/(2a), so replacing every t-difference by its matching y-difference turns the result back into the coordinates the question actually asks for.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the factor of 2 and writing t = y/a instead of t = y/(2a).
Mixing up which y-difference matches which t-difference.
steps.memory_tip: t is just y divided by 2a — swap every t-difference for its y-difference divided by 2a.

steps.label: Write the boxed area
steps.margin_note: Last mark for the boxed area — check the denominator is 8a, not 4a or 16a.
steps.why: The three factors of 2a in the denominator combine to 8a³, and one power of a² from out front cancels two of those, leaving the single power of a in the boxed answer's denominator.
common_mistakes: Losing track of how many factors of 2a appear and writing 4a or 16a in the denominator instead of 8a.
Dropping the absolute value bars, which matter here since an area cannot be negative.
steps.memory_tip: Three factors of 2a in the bottom make 8a³; the a² on top cancels two of those a's, leaving 8a in the final denominator.

insider_note: Reaching a²(t₁−t₂)(t₁−t₃)(t₂−t₃) by factoring each column of the determinant is worth showing explicitly — jumping straight from the determinant to that product without the factoring step is where marks are lost.
